nature-eco-730.title: Anaerobic oxidation of methane: the seafloor's filter
nature-eco-730.text: Little of the methane made deep under the seafloor ever reaches the water above. Anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM), or reverse methanogenesis, is the oxidation of methane by some organisms, functionally reversing {{ref:nature-eco-729}}. These organisms live in marine and freshwater settings such as methane seeps, hydrothermal vents, coastal sediments and sulfate-methane transition zones. Methanotrophs are the main reason the methane stays below.

nature-eco-731.title: Cattle and the methane they belch
nature-eco-731.text: The average cow emits around 250 liters of methane per day. In the rumen, methanogens help digest cellulose, and the methane leaves the animal mainly by belching. Ruminants contribute about 25% of anthropogenic methane emissions. A 2013 study estimated that livestock accounted for 44% of human-induced methane and about 15% of human-induced greenhouse gas emissions. One method of control is feeding ruminants 3-nitrooxypropanol.

nature-eco-741.title: The cobra effect: when a fix worsens the problem
nature-eco-741.text: In the anecdote, Delhi's government paid a bounty for dead cobras. People began breeding cobras for income, and when the scheme ended they released them, so the wild population grew. The cobra effect is a perverse result in which an apparent solution makes the problem worse. A reward for lost fishing nets on the Normandy coast in 1980-81 led people to vandalize nets to collect it. Risk compensation, the Peltzman effect, is a related case: safety measures can make people take extra risks, leaving harm unchanged or higher. All are cases of {{ref:nature-eco-740}}.

nature-eco-693.title: Plants and animals as pollution gauges
nature-eco-693.text: Some living things report pollution without any instrument. Plants and animals serve as biomonitors because their tissues or populations change measurably with pollution. Plant biomonitors include mosses, lichens, tree bark, tree rings and leaves, and tree bark can be analyzed for the pollutants it absorbed. In animals, sub-lethal effects on physiology, morphology and behavior appear long before population changes and act as early warning signals. Frogs and toads absorb toxic chemicals through permeable skin and poorly detoxify pesticides, so residues accumulate and they are used as bioindicators.

nature-eco-695.title: Stream insects and snails as water-quality witnesses
nature-eco-695.text: Almost every stream holds animals that can tell you how clean it is. Macroinvertebrates are convenient indicators of the ecological health of water bodies and terrestrial ecosystems. They are almost always present, easy to sample and identify, visible to the naked eye, short-lived and generally sedentary. They live in nearly every stream and river, including ones too shallow for fish. Some tolerate water pollution well, others do not. The EU Water Framework Directive, in force from 23 October 2000, requires all surface and groundwater bodies to be in good status. It also requires biological monitoring, which raised the use of biometrics in Europe.

nature-eco-694.title: Bacteria that signal contamination
nature-eco-694.text: Some bacteria are harmless themselves, but their presence in waste warns of other pathogens. Common indicators are total coliforms, fecal coliforms, E. coli and enterococci, and coliforms in surface water indicate fecal contamination. Microorganisms are abundant and easy to sample. Some make stress proteins when exposed to contaminants such as cadmium and benzene, an early warning. Helminth eggs indicate the safety of wastewater reuse because they are the most resistant pathogens and survive 10-12 months in tropical climates.

nature-eco-744.title: Bush control: thinning shrubs without wiping them out
nature-eco-744.text: Managing bushes means shaping how dense they are and what they are made of, to cut risks such as wildfire or to rehabilitate land. The aim for encroaching native woody plants is to reduce them, not eradicate them. Methods are controlled fire, herbicides and mechanical cutting, which is followed by burning or browsing to stop regrowth. Funding is a key constraint. Selling harvested woody biomass, such as charcoal in Namibia, can pay for restoration.

nature-eco-723.title: Carbon from outside versus carbon from within
nature-eco-723.text: A lake can feed on its own algae or on what washes in. Allochthonous carbon and nutrients come from outside an aquatic system, while autochthonous carbon comes from within it, such as algae. In streams and small lakes allochthonous sources dominate. In large lakes and the ocean, autochthonous sources dominate. Allochthony is the share of aquatic food web biomass derived from allochthonous material.

nature-eco-725.title: Oxygen in water: made by light, spent by life
nature-eco-725.text: Dissolved oxygen in water is raised by photosynthesis and wind mixing and lowered by aerobic respiration. In the dark only respiration occurs. The balance between oxygen production and consumption is the aquatic metabolism rate. Temperature matters too: warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen because solubility depends on temperature.

nature-eco-722.title: Classifying lakes by nutrients: from clear to green
nature-eco-722.text: Lakes can be classified by a trophic state index, according to their nutrient levels and primary production. Oligotrophic lakes have low nutrients and primary production. Eutrophic lakes have very high nutrients and productivity, and can suffer algal blooms. Dystrophic lakes have high humic matter and yellow-brown, tea-colored waters. The categories have no rigid specifications; they form a spectrum.

nature-eco-724.title: Phosphorus, the nutrient that limits lake growth
nature-eco-724.text: Phosphorus is a limiting factor for phytoplankton growth because its concentration in water is generally low. Dissolved phosphorus is often very limiting to primary productivity in freshwater. Nitrogen is a different story. Most organisms avoid dissolved N2 because it takes high energy to use, so water quality studies focus on nitrate, nitrite and ammonia.

nature-eco-726.title: Tropical lakes and rivers compared with temperate ones
nature-eco-726.text: Tropical limnology studies the physical, chemical, biological and cultural aspects of freshwater systems in tropical regions. Tropical waters have warmer, more stable temperatures and higher nutrient levels than temperate ones. Freshwater biodiversity there is typically higher, and human impacts are often more severe.

nature-eco-686.title: The aridity index: measuring how dry a climate is
nature-eco-686.text:
Aridity is permanent, whereas drought is temporary. An aridity index is a numerical indicator of how dry the climate is at a given place. Indices serve to identify and delimit regions with a water deficit that can severely limit land use. The 1992 UNEP index relates potential evapotranspiration to average annual precipitation, both in the same units. It increases with wetter conditions, so some hydrologists call it a humidity index.

UNEP classes run from drier to wetter. Hyperarid is below 0.05, covering 7.5% of global land. Arid is 0.05-0.20 (12.1%), semi-arid 0.20-0.50 (17.7%) and dry subhumid 0.50-0.65 (9.9%).
